page.title: Minting unique IDs
page.kicker: Lecture 06 · week 3, day 2 · running case: one getid() function
page.dek: Rewrite one getid() function under ever harder constraints, then see how Amazon, Flickr, Twitter and Instagram answer the same question.
page.description: Lecture 06: rewrite one getid() function under harder constraints, then see how Amazon, Flickr, Twitter Snowflake and Instagram mint unique IDs, and why good IDs make pagination fast.

chapters.title: Why build your own IDs
chapters.summary: Every database already hands out IDs. Here is the moment that stops being enough, and the question this whole lecture answers.

chapters.title: Building getid(), one constraint at a time
chapters.summary: One function, six versions. Each new condition (another machine, threads, a reboot, a busy disk) breaks the last version, and the smallest change fixes it.

chapters.title: Order, and why clocks break it
chapters.summary: Some systems need to know which ID came first. Putting time on the left almost does it. Real clocks, and the need for more than one server, are why "almost" is as good as it gets.

chapters.title: How big should an ID be?
chapters.summary: A UUID is unique with no coordination at all. The companies in this lecture still turned it down, and the reason is the index.

chapters.title: Central services: Amazon and Flickr
chapters.summary: Two ways to make one place responsible for IDs without making every request wait on it: Amazon hands out ranges, Flickr turns MySQL's auto-increment into a ticket machine.

chapters.title: Snowflake: IDs without a service
chapters.summary: Twitter's 64-bit layout puts time, machine and counter in one integer, with no service in the path. Discord and Sony reuse it with a different start date.

chapters.title: Instagram: Snowflake inside the database
chapters.summary: Same idea, different home. Instagram packed time, shard and sequence into 64 bits inside a database function, so no API server knows anything about IDs.

chapters.title: Pagination: the side effect
chapters.summary: IDs with time on the left can be compared, and tables are kept in key order. Together they make "the next page" cost the same at page 1 and page 1,000.

chapters.title: What to keep
chapters.summary: Strict order or throughput, where the ID is born, and the habits this lecture keeps returning to.
